Based on my chemical knowledge, I can analyze this question:

In nitrate (NO3-) and nitrite (NO2-) salts, the reactivity is influenced by the properties of the cation. Let me analyze each option:

A. Alkali metals (Na+, K+) - These form ionic bonds with nitrate/nitrite ions. The resulting salts are generally stable and less reactive because alkali metals have low charge density and do not participate in redox reactions with the nitrate/nitrite anions.

B. Alkaline earth metals (Ca2+, Mg2+) - Similar to alkali metals but with a 2+ charge. They form relatively stable nitrate/nitrite salts, though slightly more reactive than alkali metal salts due to higher charge density.

C. Noble gases (Ar, Ne) - Noble gases don't form cations under normal conditions due to their filled electron shells, so this option is incorrect.

D. Transition metals (Fe2+/3+, Cu2+) - Transition metal cations generally make nitrate/nitrite salts more reactive because:
   - They have variable oxidation states and can participate in redox reactions
   - They can act as catalysts for the decomposition of nitrates/nitrites
   - They form coordination complexes with nitrate/nitrite ions
   - Their nitrate salts are generally stronger oxidizing agents
   - They have higher charge densities which can polarize the N-O bonds

Transition metal nitrates like copper nitrate Cu(NO3)2 and iron nitrate Fe(NO3)3 are known to be stronger oxidizing agents than alkali metal nitrates like NaNO3 or KNO3. They decompose more readily upon heating and are more reactive in various chemical processes.
